questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/54153dcd97ac6471956b6db34f175d1ee622c9bf74e85f93d5e303a7842d24ed.png)

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.

$$
{(x,y)\in {{field-1}}\,:\,{{field-2}}<x<{{field-3}},\,{{field-4}}<y<{{field-5}}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
A point $P(x,y)$ lies inside the rectangle if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
\begin{aligned}2<x<6,\,2<y<5\end{aligned}
$$

Moreover, since *every* real value in these intervals is included, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write our set as follows:

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,2<x<6,\,\,2<y<5}
$$

Describe the set of points shown above using set-builder notation.

$$
{(x,y)\in {{field-1}}\,:\,{{field-2}}\le x\le {{field-3}},\,{{field-4}}\le y\le {{field-5}}}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Since all points $P(x,y)$ in our set lie at integer values of $x$ and $y,$ we have $x\in Z,y\in Z,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in Z\times Z={Z}^{2}.
$$

The points $P(x,y)$ satisfy the condition

$$
x\in {-1,0,1,2},\,y\in {-2,-1,0,1,2,3}.
$$

In other words,

$$
-1\le x\le 2,\,-2\le y\le 3.
$$

Therefore, we can write our set as follows:

$$
{(x,y)\in {Z}^{2}\,:\,-1\le x\le 2,\,-2\le y\le 3}
$$

The points in our set include all those that lie *below* the line $y=x-1.$ For those points, the following condition is satisfied:

$$

Therefore, we can write the set as follows:

$$

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.

$$
{(x,y)\in {{field-1}}\,:\,-2\,{{field-2}}\,y\,{{field-3}}\,x}
$$
questions.worked_solution:
The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=-2$ and *below* the line $y=x.$

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y>-2,\,y<x.
$$

 

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
-2<y<x
$$

Since the boundary is not included in the set (the lines are dashed), the inequalities are strict.

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in R,y\in R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in R\times R={R}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,-2<y<x}.
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Describing Non-Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation
questions.worked_solution:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=4$ and vertical radius $b=3.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{9} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=144.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(0,4).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
9(0)^{2}+16(4)^{2}\,>\,144.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}>144.
$$

Notice that we use $>$ since the boundary is excluded from the set (the boundary curve is dashed).

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}>144}.
$$

The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{a}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{b}^{2}}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=4$ and vertical radius $b=2.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{16}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{4} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(5,0).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
4(5)^{2}+16(0)^{2}\,>\,64.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}>64.
$$

We must also include the curve $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}\ge 64.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
{(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,:\,4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}\ge 64}.
$$

Describe the set of points shown above using set-builder notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since all points $P(x,y)$ in our set lie at integer values of $x$ and $y,$ we have $x\in \mathbb Z, y\in\mathbb Z,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in \mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z^2.
$$

The points $P(x,y)$ satisfy the condition

$$
x \in \{1,2,3\}, \quad y \in \{ -3,-2,-1,0,1,2 \}.
$$

In other words,

$$
1 \leq x \leq 3, \quad -3 \leq y \leq 2
$$

Therefore, we can write our set as follows:

$$
\Big\{ (x,y)  \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z^2}
\: : \: 
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}  
\leq  x \leq  
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}3} , \: 
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}-3}  
\leq  y \leq  
\bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}2} 
\Big\}.
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/787b62fbe367feae9e4c8ed10b983a256840e3a93727fea7c1ff67cacad0129d.png)

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Since all points $P(x,y)$ in our set lie at integer values of $x$ and $y,$ we have $x\in \mathbb Z, y\in\mathbb Z,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in \mathbb Z\times\mathbb Z = \mathbb Z^2.
$$

The points in our set include all those that lie *below* the line $y=x+2.$ For those points, the following condition is satisfied:

$$
y \lt x+2
$$

Also, notice that some points in our set lie *on* the line. We include these points by changing the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as follows:

$$
\Big\{(x,y) \in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb Z ^2} \: : \: y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq }x+2 \Big\}
$$

canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/45260087c5196cc239f21402d73169f60139bd7d2c10ee0aa1db4e1a2c56be4a.png)

Describe the shaded region shown above using set-builder notation.
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The points in our set include all those that lie *above* the line $y=2x$ and *below* the line $y=3.$

A point $P(x,y)$ lies *inside* the shaded region if the following conditions are satisfied:

$$
y \gt 2x, \qquad y < 3.
$$

Combining this into a single condition, we have

$$
2x \lt y < 3.
$$

We must also include the line $y= 3$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the corresponding inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
2x \lt y  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3
$$

Moreover, since we're considering *every* real value in this region, $x\in \mathbb R, y\in\mathbb R,$ and therefore 

$$
(x,y)\in \mathbb R\times\mathbb R = \mathbb R^2.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
\Big\{(x,y)\in \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\mathbb R^2 } \: : \:  2x \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\lt } y \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\leq } 3 \Big\}.
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Describing Non-Rectangular Sets Using Set-Builder Notation
canonical_examples.problem:
Use set builder notation to describe the shaded region given in the diagram below:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14096165/assets/e5f5f2f2e67ba0ad566b2759ca5536d248f671bf0f082d567a7f7d993772601e.png)
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The equation of an ellipse centered at the origin with a horizontal radius of length $a$ and a vertical radius of length $b$ is given by

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}+\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=1.
$$

 

Here, the elliptical boundary of our region has horizontal radius $a=5$ and vertical radius $b=4.$ Therefore, the equation of the ellipse is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{{x}^{2}}{25}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{16} & =1,\end{aligned}
$$

which we can write as

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400.
$$

We're interested in describing all points that lie *outside* the ellipse. So, let's pick any point outside the region, say, $(10,0).$ Substituting its coordinates into the equation of the boundary, we obtain

$$
16(10)^2+25(0)^2 \: {\color{blue}>} \: 400.
$$

As a result, the points $P(x,y)$ in our region are any real numbers that satisfy the condition

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2  \gt 400.
$$

We must also include the curve $16x^2 + 25y^2 = 400$ since the boundary is included in the set (the curve is solid). So, we change the inequality symbol above as follows:

$$
16x^2 + 25y^2  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400.
$$

Therefore, we can write the set as

$$
\Big\{(x,y) \in \mathbb{R}^2 \: : \: \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}16 }x^2 + \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}25 }y^2  \bbox[2pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}\geq } 400 \bigg\}.
$$
